title: S&P Global
workingHypotheses: The strongest narrative tension is translating expert financial logic without flattening its power.

organisingIdea.statement: Make index logic visible and teachable without taking authorship or expert control away from the people building it.

claims.statement: The engagement aimed to turn an index-building workflow based on email, spreadsheets, Python scripts, and undocumented expert knowledge into a visual product.

sources.locator: pp. 5–6, Factsheet and Behind the Brief

claims.notes: Confirm the product's exact public name.

claims.statement: The intended audience included experienced financial experts and newer users; research participants included analysts, hedge-fund managers, and index engineers.
claims.notes: Clarify the actual primary user and purchasing audience.

claims.statement: Alexander led UX and visual design and contributed workflow mapping, interface language, screens, flows, prototypes, workshops, and user-test facilitation.
claims.notes: Separate leadership, hands-on production, and shared team responsibilities in interview.

claims.statement: The old portfolio credits Tom Good, Claudia Carbutt, Andy Kemp, and Martin Grosjean and describes collaboration with a UX lead and junior designer.
claims.notes: Confirm spelling, titles, and permission to credit.

claims.statement: The team had to preserve the depth of a system built for internal experts while making it understandable to external users, with few comparable products to reference.
claims.notes: Strong candidate for the opening tension.

claims.statement: Foundation, schedule, and method were represented as modular, swappable building blocks so users could see how an index was assembled.
claims.notes: Confirm whether this model shipped and how it evolved.

claims.statement: Internal working sessions established a shared model, and later walkthroughs with power users helped tune defaults, grouping, and progressive disclosure.
claims.notes: Ask for one specific piece of feedback and the design change it caused.

claims.statement: Interface language, micro-animation, typography, and restrained colour were used to make a dense product feel lighter without concealing data.
claims.notes: The language insight is narratively useful but needs a concrete before-and-after example.

claims.statement: The old portfolio claims the platform reduced index launch time from three weeks to a few days.
claims.notes: Do not publish without method, baseline, and client confirmation.

claims.statement: Portfolio v1 shows a detailed rule-builder interface and describes a separate SPICE marketing rollout as ongoing in May 2025.
claims.notes: Clarify what shipped, what was prototype, and whether SPICE belongs in the same case study.

conflicts.question: Should the project be named S&P Global, S&P Dow Jones Index Builder, or SPICE Index Builder, and is the CV's 'SMP Global' simply a typo?

openQuestions.question: What exactly was the product, who used it, and what was the original problem?
What did Alexander personally own and make, and what belonged to the wider team?
Which rule, validation problem, or interaction decision best demonstrates the difficult work?
Who were the closest collaborators and how did they change the work?
What shipped or changed, and can any speed or workflow improvement be substantiated?
